title: 2024 AMC 8 Problem 7
statement: A \(3 \times 7\) rectangle is covered without overlap by \(3\) shapes of tiles: \(2 \times 2,\) \(1 \times 4,\) and \(1 \times 1,\) shown below. What is the minimum possible number of \(1 \times 1\) tiles used?

solutions.text:
The \(2\times2\) and \(1\times4\) tiles each have area \(4\). Since the rectangle has area \(21\), the number of \(1\times1\) tiles must be congruent to \(1\pmod4\). Among the choices, only \(1\) and \(5\) are possible by area.

It is impossible to use just one \(1\times1\) tile. If the larger tiles covered the other \(20\) cells, then two rows would have all \(7\) cells covered by larger tiles. But each \(2\times2\) tile covers \(2\) cells in any row it meets, and each \(1\times4\) tile covers \(4\) cells in one row, so each row would have an even number of cells covered by larger tiles. A row cannot have \(7\) such cells.

The following tiling shows that \(5\) unit tiles are possible.

Thus, E is the correct answer.
hints: The area left for non-unit tiles must be a multiple of \(4\)
If only one unit tile were used, two rows would need an odd number of cells covered by larger tiles
